summary: Sync must delete activity occurrences inside the fetched window that it did not see, not only upsert the ones it did. Because that deletes user-visible rows, it runs ONLY when the seen set is a complete account of the window. Completeness is easy to believe and easy to get wrong: it requires every profile (so --profile blocks pruning outright), both activities and calendar_events synced with no record-level failures, and no --max-pages truncation.
reason: Upsert-only mirroring leaves a row behind forever when an activity is deleted, moved to another day, or dropped from a recurrence, and every offline read (agenda, feed, backup, capacity, overlaps, drift) then reports a plan the user no longer has. There was no other cure: --full re-fetches but never deletes, so the only way to clear a stale row was deleting the database file. Three properties of this schema force the implementation and must survive a regen. (1) The occurrence date is recoverable ONLY by parsing the storage key: the activities table has a `date` column but nothing populates it, because the day comes from the response map key rather than any field of the activity JSON. (2) Victim selection and key comparison must happen in Go and deletes must be issued by integer rowid, because occurrence keys embed a NUL and SQLite's string functions stop at the first one. (3) Externally-imported calendar events are written into the SAME activities table by a different endpoint behind a different selector, so pruning after an activities-only sync would delete every imported event. The store's ReconcilePartition cannot be reused: it compares BareResourceID, which strips the occurrence suffix, so all occurrences of one activity collapse to one identity. Two ways the seen set silently goes partial were found in review and are the reason the guard list is this long. (1) `--profile` narrows the profile list BEFORE the sync loop, so the union-across-profiles accumulation unions exactly one profile while the sweep still covers the shared table -- the very hazard the union exists to prevent, reintroduced by a flag. Activity rows carry no profile column, so the sweep cannot be narrowed to compensate; refusing to prune is the only correct answer. (2) syncCalendarEvents skipped per-record failures with a bare `continue`, so it could return success while some occurrences never entered the seen set, and pruning then deleted those rows as stale. Any record a run failed to account for must make that run non-authoritative. (3) A hidden or disconnected external calendar is skipped by syncCalendarEvents, so its previously mirrored events never reach the seen set either. Hiding a calendar in the app is a display preference, not a deletion, so pruning on that basis would silently destroy its mirrored history. Rows carry the calendar they came from, so those rows are re-affirmed into the seen set instead of blocking the whole run; if they cannot be re-affirmed, the run is marked non-authoritative. The completeness proof also has to flow INTO the pruner, not just gate the call: deleting the last activity in a window legitimately yields an empty seen set, so a blanket 'empty means no evidence' rule would leave that final removed occurrence visible forever. pruneStaleOccurrences therefore takes an explicit windowVerified argument -- empty plus verified prunes, empty without it is still treated as no evidence, because an empty response is also the shape a silent upstream failure takes.
validated_outcome: Unit tests cover occurrence-level granularity (two occurrences of one activity, only the unseen one deleted), window bounds (an occurrence outside [from,to] is never a victim), the generic resources mirror that backs backup and export being swept alongside the typed table, and each guard in canPruneOccurrences. An empty seen-set is treated as no evidence and deletes nothing, so a run that recorded nothing cannot erase the mirror. Pruning failure is reported on stderr and never fails the sync, because the records written are still correct. Guard tests additionally cover the --profile refusal (asserting the reason names the flag, so the message stays actionable) and a failed calendar_events resource. Both holes were caught in maintainer review, not by the live gate -- neither is reachable from a default `sync` against a single-profile account, which is exactly what the gate exercises. A further test covers the hidden-calendar case: rows belonging to a skipped calendar survive, rows of a different calendar and native activities the run did not see are still pruned. Note the pattern across all three holes -- they are all the same mistake, skipping work without recording that it was skipped, and pruning cannot distinguish that from an upstream deletion.
